The paper presents an automated system for detecting visual damages on wind turbine blades.
The system is based on a Mask R-CNN model trained on over 250,000 inspection pictures with 370,000+ annotations.
The model was trained on a p3.2x large AWS EC2 instance with a NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU.
On a test set of 18,318 images, the model achieved a damage recall of 94.4% and a damage precision of 40.48%.
The model generates 'clues' which are the tightest bounding boxes around the predicted damage areas, and presents them to human analysts for review.
In A/B testing, the analysts using the automated system had reduced average time for quality checks and fewer missed damages compared to the previous manual process.
Future work includes improving the bounding box shapes, training on segmented blade images, and exploring real-time inference on the drone.
Detecting wind turbine blade damages early is critical for reducing the high operational costs of wind energy and enabling it to be cost-competitive with fossil fuels.
Blade damages are the leading cause of wind turbine failures during operations.

The paper argues for prioritizing the actual values and needs of end-users (analysts) in designing and evaluating the automated system, rather than just optimizing traditional machine learning metrics.
The automated system is part of a commercialized product aimed at enabling more automated wind farms.
Over 90,000 wind turbines have been inspected across more than 26 countries using the system.
The inspection pictures are captured using a Sony UMC-R10C camera with a resolution of 5456x3632.
The ground truth damage annotations are provided by trained human analysts.
The model was trained on down-sampled 1500x998 resolution images due to the large original size.
